claim: The basal forebrain features distinct connectivity along its rostrocaudal axis.
source: Although often treated as a monolithic structure, the basal forebrain features distinct connectivity along its rostrocaudal axis that could impart regional differences in BFCN processing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known anatomical fact that motivates the study.

claim: BFCNs in both HDB and GP/SI regions showed equivalently weak responses to unconditioned visual stimuli.
source: BFCNs in both regions showed equivalently weak responses to unconditioned visual stimuli and anticipated rewards.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: BFCNs in both HDB and GP/SI regions showed equivalently weak responses to anticipated rewards.
source: BFCNs in both regions showed equivalently weak responses to unconditioned visual stimuli and anticipated rewards.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: Rostral BFCNs in the horizontal limb of the diagonal band were more responsive to reward omission.
source: Rostral BFCNs in the horizontal limb of the diagonal band were more responsive to reward omission, more accurately classified behavioral outcomes, and more closely tracked fluctuations in pupil-indexed global brain state.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: Rostral BFCNs in HDB more accurately classified behavioral outcomes.
source: Rostral BFCNs in the horizontal limb of the diagonal band were more responsive to reward omission, more accurately classified behavioral outcomes, and more closely tracked fluctuations in pupil-indexed global brain state.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B and 4D.

claim: Rostral BFCNs in HDB more closely tracked fluctuations in pupil-indexed global brain state.
source: Rostral BFCNs in the horizontal limb of the diagonal band were more responsive to reward omission, more accurately classified behavioral outcomes, and more closely tracked fluctuations in pupil-indexed global brain state.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: Caudal tail BFCNs in GP/SI were more responsive to unconditioned auditory stimuli.
source: Caudal tail BFCNs in globus pallidus and substantia innominata were more responsive to unconditioned auditory stimuli, orofacial movements, aversive reinforcement, and showed robust associative plasticity for punishment-predicting cues.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Caudal tail BFCNs in GP/SI were more responsive to orofacial movements.
source: Caudal tail BFCNs in globus pallidus and substantia innominata were more responsive to unconditioned auditory stimuli, orofacial movements, aversive reinforcement, and showed robust associative plasticity for punishment-predicting cues.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Caudal tail BFCNs in GP/SI were more responsive to aversive reinforcement.
source: Caudal tail BFCNs in globus pallidus and substantia innominata were more responsive to unconditioned auditory stimuli, orofacial movements, aversive reinforcement, and showed robust associative plasticity for punishment-predicting cues.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: Caudal tail BFCNs in GP/SI showed robust associative plasticity for punishment-predicting cues.
source: Caudal tail BFCNs in globus pallidus and substantia innominata were more responsive to unconditioned auditory stimuli, orofacial movements, aversive reinforcement, and showed robust associative plasticity for punishment-predicting cues.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7C.

claim: BFCNs in HDB feature strong reciprocal connectivity with prefrontal cortex and lateral hypothalamus.
source: BFCNs in rostral structures such as the horizontal limb of the diagonal band of Broca (HDB) feature strong reciprocal connectivity with prefrontal cortex and lateral hypothalamus, with additional projections to entorhinal cortex, olfactory bulb, and pyriform cortex (Bloem et al., 2014; Gielow and Zaborszky, 2017; Li et al., 2018; Rye et al., 1984; Zaborszky et al., 2012; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: BFCNs in HDB have additional projections to entorhinal cortex, olfactory bulb, and pyriform cortex.
source: BFCNs in rostral structures such as the horizontal limb of the diagonal band of Broca (HDB) feature strong reciprocal connectivity with prefrontal cortex and lateral hypothalamus, with additional projections to entorhinal cortex, olfactory bulb, and pyriform cortex (Bloem et al., 2014; Gielow and Zaborszky, 2017; Li et al., 2018; Rye et al., 1984; Zaborszky et al., 2012; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: BFCNs at GP/SI receive strong inputs from the caudate putamen, the medial geniculate, and posterior intrathalamic nuclei.
source: By contrast, BFCNs at the caudal tail of the basal forebrain, at the intersection of globus pallidus and substantia innominata (GP/SI), receive strong inputs from the caudate putamen, the medial geniculate, and posterior intrathalamic nuclei, and are the primary source of cholinergic input to the auditory cortex (ACtx), with comparatively weak projections to frontal cortical areas (Chavez and Zaborszky, 2017; Guo et al., 2019; Kamke et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2016; Rye et al., 1984; Zaborszky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: BFCNs at GP/SI are the primary source of cholinergic input to the auditory cortex.
source: By contrast, BFCNs at the caudal tail of the basal forebrain, at the intersection of globus pallidus and substantia innominata (GP/SI), receive strong inputs from the caudate putamen, the medial geniculate, and posterior intrathalamic nuclei, and are the primary source of cholinergic input to the auditory cortex (ACtx), with comparatively weak projections to frontal cortical areas (Chavez and Zaborszky, 2017; Guo et al., 2019; Kamke et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2016; Rye et al., 1984; Zaborszky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: BFCNs at GP/SI have comparatively weak projections to frontal cortical areas.
source: By contrast, BFCNs at the caudal tail of the basal forebrain, at the intersection of globus pallidus and substantia innominata (GP/SI), receive strong inputs from the caudate putamen, the medial geniculate, and posterior intrathalamic nuclei, and are the primary source of cholinergic input to the auditory cortex (ACtx), with comparatively weak projections to frontal cortical areas (Chavez and Zaborszky, 2017; Guo et al., 2019; Kamke et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2016; Rye et al., 1984; Zaborszky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: GCaMP expression was almost entirely restricted to cholinergic neurons within the HDB and GP/SI.
source: We confirmed that GCaMP expression was almost entirely restricted to cholinergic neurons within the HDB and GP/SI by immunolabeling regions near the end of the fiber tips for ChAT in a subset of implanted mice (N = 4, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for a presentation of all 22 fiber tip locations in 11 mice).
evidence: This is confirmed by immunohistochemical data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: ChAT-negative neurons that expressed GCaMP were rare in HDB, amounting to just 95/1719 (5.5%).
source: ChAT-negative neurons that expressed GCaMP were rare, amounting to just 95/1719 in HDB (5.5%) and 48/764 in GP/SI (6.3%) (Figure 1D, left).
evidence: This is quantified from immunohistochemical data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: ChAT-negative neurons that expressed GCaMP were rare in GP/SI, amounting to just 48/764 (6.3%).
source: ChAT-negative neurons that expressed GCaMP were rare, amounting to just 95/1719 in HDB (5.5%) and 48/764 in GP/SI (6.3%) (Figure 1D, left).
evidence: This is quantified from immunohistochemical data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: GCaMP coherence with pupil fluctuations was significantly higher in HDB than GP/SI.
source: GCaMP coherence with pupil fluctuations was significantly higher in HDB than GP/SI, where bulk calcium dynamics could account for as much as 80% of the variability in slow pupil changes (Figure 1F, statistical reporting provided in figure legends).
evidence: This is demonstrated by coherence analysis presented in Figure 1F with statistical support.

claim: Bulk calcium dynamics in HDB could account for as much as 80% of the variability in slow pupil changes.
source: GCaMP coherence with pupil fluctuations was significantly higher in HDB than GP/SI, where bulk calcium dynamics could account for as much as 80% of the variability in slow pupil changes (Figure 1F, statistical reporting provided in figure legends).
evidence: This is inferred from the coherence data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: GCaMP signals led pupil dilations by approximately 0.7 s.
source: The timing of correlated GCaMP transients and pupil dilations were similar across brain areas, where GCaMP signals led pupil dilations by approximately 0.7 s (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is measured from cross-correlation analysis presented in Figure 1G.

claim: Coherence between ACtx ACh3.0 fluorescence and pupil fluctuations strongly resembled GCaMP coherence from GP/SI cell bodies.
source: As expected, coherence between ACtx ACh3.0 fluorescence and pupil fluctuations strongly resembled GCaMP coherence from GP/SI cell bodies, both in terms of the strong coherence with slow (<0.1 Hz) changes in pupil diameter (Figure 1I) and in terms of timing, where ACh3.0 signal surges led pupil dilations by approximately 0.6 s (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by coherence analysis comparing ACh3.0 sensor data with GCaMP data, presented in Figures 1I and 1J.

claim: ACh3.0 signal surges led pupil dilations by approximately 0.6 s.
source: As expected, coherence between ACtx ACh3.0 fluorescence and pupil fluctuations strongly resembled GCaMP coherence from GP/SI cell bodies, both in terms of the strong coherence with slow (<0.1 Hz) changes in pupil diameter (Figure 1I) and in terms of timing, where ACh3.0 signal surges led pupil dilations by approximately 0.6 s (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is measured from cross-correlation analysis presented in Figure 1J.

claim: BFCN responses to unconditioned auditory stimuli were markedly different than visual stimuli.
source: BFCN responses to unconditioned auditory stimuli were markedly different than visual stimuli, as observed for both complex broadband ripple sounds (Figure 2C, middle) and brief pure tone pips (Figure 2C, bottom).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing response amplitudes in Figure 2C.

claim: In GP/SI, significant BFCN responses were observed for both types of sounds at all stimulus intensities.
source: In GP/SI, significant BFCN responses were observed for both types of sounds at all stimulus intensities and were all significantly greater than the corresponding HDB responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2C with statistical comparisons.

claim: GP/SI BFCN responses to sounds were all significantly greater than the corresponding HDB responses.
source: In GP/SI, significant BFCN responses were observed for both types of sounds at all stimulus intensities and were all significantly greater than the corresponding HDB responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2C with statistical comparisons.

claim: Large pupil dilations to the first presentation of an auditory ripple at 70 dB SPL habituated to approximately 50% of their initial amplitude after one or two trials.
source: Along these lines, we observed large pupil dilations to the first presentation of an auditory ripple at 70 dB SPL, which then habituated to approximately 50% of their initial amplitude after one or two trials, presumably reflecting the loss of stimulus novelty (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the habituation data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Ripple-evoked BFCN responses decreased by approximately 30% after the first presentation before stabilizing at approximately 60% of the initial amplitude across subsequent presentations.
source: Ripple-evoked BFCN responses decayed in parallel with pupil responses, where responses decreased by approximately 30% after the first presentation before stabilizing at approximately 60% of the initial amplitude across subsequent presentations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the habituation data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: The proportional decay of ripple-evoked responses with habituation was equivalent in GP/SI and HDB.
source: Although the ripple-evoked response amplitude was greater overall in GP/SI than HDB, the proportional decay with habituation was equivalent (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the habituation data presented in Figure 2E with statistical analysis.

claim: The amplitude of spontaneous GCaMP transients was unchanged throughout the recording period.
source: We found that the amplitude of spontaneous GCaMP transients was unchanged throughout the recording period, confirming that the reduced sensory-evoked GCaMP responses over the test session reflected habituation to stimulus novelty (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the control data presented in Figure 2F.

claim: All mice learned the appetitive detection task within a few sessions.
source: Although the rates of procedural learning varied somewhat between mice (Figure 3B), all mice learned the task within a few sessions and either detected the tone to receive reward (hit) or failed to lick at all in response to the tone (miss), with very few instances of partial hits (>0 but <7 licks in 2.8 s) observed after the first few behavioral sessions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the learning curves presented in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Tone-evoked responses were not greatly changed late in training, after mice had learned the stimulus-reward association.
source: On average, tone-evoked responses were not greatly changed late in training, after mice had learned the stimulus-reward association (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing early and late training responses in Figures 3F-G.

claim: BFCN responses to reward-predicting tones did not significantly change over the course of learning for hit or miss trials in either brain area.
source: Overall, BFCN responses to reward-predicting tones did not significantly change over the course of learning for hit or miss trials in either brain area (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the learning-related analysis presented in Figure 3H with statistical support.

claim: Cue-evoked responses were strongly reduced in HDB and GP/SI on miss trials.
source: Cue-evoked responses were strongly reduced in HDB and GP/SI on miss trials (Figure 3D–H), although this difference is confounded by the potential contribution of lick-related motor activity that would only occur on hit trials.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing hit and miss trial responses in Figures 3D-H.

claim: Mean BFCN activity measured in a 1 s period prior to cue onset was significantly elevated on miss trials in both structures.
source: We found that mean BFCN activity measured in a 1 s period prior to cue onset was significantly elevated on miss trials in both structures, though the difference was significantly greater in HDB (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the baseline activity analysis presented in Figure 3I with statistical support.

claim: The difference in pre-cue baseline activity between hit and miss trials was significantly greater in HDB than GP/SI.
source: We found that mean BFCN activity measured in a 1 s period prior to cue onset was significantly elevated on miss trials in both structures, though the difference was significantly greater in HDB (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the baseline activity analysis presented in Figure 3I with statistical support.

claim: Differences in both pre- and post-cue BFCN activity supported classification of behavioral trial outcome with an accuracy that was significantly greater than a randomized control assignment for all brain structures.
source: Despite the limited spatial and temporal resolution of GCaMP fiber imaging, differences in both pre- and post-cue BFCN activity supported classification of behavioral trial outcome with an accuracy that was significantly greater than a randomized control assignment for all brain structures (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SVM classification analysis presented in Figures 4B and 4D with statistical support.

claim: For either pre- and post-cue activity, the HDB fiber classification accuracy was significantly higher than GP/SI.
source: For either pre- and post-cue activity, the HDB fiber classification accuracy was significantly higher than GP/SI and was not significantly different than the combined activity from both fibers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SVM classification analysis presented in Figures 4B and 4D with statistical support.

claim: HDB fiber classification accuracy was not significantly different than the combined activity from both fibers.
source: For either pre- and post-cue activity, the HDB fiber classification accuracy was significantly higher than GP/SI and was not significantly different than the combined activity from both fibers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SVM classification analysis presented in Figures 4B and 4D with statistical support.

claim: BFCN responses to the onset of licks increased monotonically across lick bout duration.
source: BFCN responses to the onset of licks increased monotonically across lick bout duration and, while fairly modest overall (i.e., when compared to cue-evoked responses), were significantly greater in GP/SI than HDB (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lick-related activity analysis presented in Figure 5B with statistical support.

claim: BFCN responses to the onset of licks were significantly greater in GP/SI than HDB.
source: BFCN responses to the onset of licks increased monotonically across lick bout duration and, while fairly modest overall (i.e., when compared to cue-evoked responses), were significantly greater in GP/SI than HDB (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lick-related activity analysis presented in Figure 5B with statistical support.

claim: False alarm events during the inter-trial interval were uncommon overall, mostly occurring mid-way through the operant learning task.
source: False alarm events during the inter-trial interval were uncommon overall, mostly occurring mid-way through the operant learning task (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the false alarm incidence data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Elevated BFCN activity prior to cue onset in undetected miss trials was not observed prior to false alarm events.
source: Unlike the elevated BFCN activity prior to cue onset in undetected miss trials (Figure 3I), we did not observe a commensurate elevation in BFCN activity prior to false alarm events, suggesting that changes in baseline activity levels are more closely related to perceptual accuracy than behavioral action (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing pre-event activity for different trial types in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Changes in baseline BFCN activity levels are more closely related to perceptual accuracy than behavioral action.
source: Unlike the elevated BFCN activity prior to cue onset in undetected miss trials (Figure 3I), we did not observe a commensurate elevation in BFCN activity prior to false alarm events, suggesting that changes in baseline activity levels are more closely related to perceptual accuracy than behavioral action (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of baseline activity patterns across different trial types.

claim: Phasic responses at the cessation of licking were only observed when lick bouts exceeded the threshold for a false alarm event.
source: We also noted phasic responses at the cessation of licking, but only when lick bouts exceeded the threshold for a false alarm event (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lick offset analysis presented in Figure 5C.

claim: In HDB, significantly greater responses were observed at the offset of lick bouts, but only when ≥7 licks were produced.
source: In HDB, which exhibited comparatively weak responses to movement onset, we observed significantly greater responses at the offset of lick bouts, but only when ≥7 licks were produced (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lick offset analysis presented in Figures 5D-E with statistical support.

claim: Phasic responses at the offset of false alarm events may reflect a reward omission response.
source: In this scenario, phasic responses at the offset of false alarm events may reflect a reward omission response.
evidence: This is proposed as an interpretation of the observed data pattern.

claim: Go responses to the tone associated with a neutral outcome were reduced to approximately 40% of trials within a few behavioral sessions.
source: Within a few behavioral sessions, Go responses to the tone associated with a neutral outcome were reduced to approximately 40% of trials and Go response to the tone associated with tongue shock was only observed on approximately 25% of trials (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the behavioral learning data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Go response to the tone associated with tongue shock was only observed on approximately 25% of trials within a few behavioral sessions.
source: Within a few behavioral sessions, Go responses to the tone associated with a neutral outcome were reduced to approximately 40% of trials and Go response to the tone associated with tongue shock was only observed on approximately 25% of trials (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the behavioral learning data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: BFCN responses to anticipated rewards were very weak in both HDB and GP/SI.
source: We observed that BFCN responses to anticipated rewards were very weak in both HDB and GP/SI (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the reinforcement-related response analysis presented in Figure 6E.

claim: The omission of an anticipated reward was associated with a moderate response in HDB that was significantly greater than both reward delivery response from the same fiber and the reward omission response in GP/SI.
source: The omission of an anticipated reward was associated with a moderate response in HDB that was significantly greater than both reward delivery response from the same fiber and the reward omission response in GP/SI.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the reinforcement-related response analysis presented in Figure 6E with statistical support.

claim: Delivery of silent, noxious stimulus elicited the strongest BFCN responses in both regions.
source: Delivery of silent, noxious stimulus elicited the strongest BFCN responses in both regions, although the response to shock was significantly greater in GP/SI than HDB (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the reinforcement-related response analysis presented in Figure 6E with statistical support.

claim: The response to shock was significantly greater in GP/SI than HDB.
source: Delivery of silent, noxious stimulus elicited the strongest BFCN responses in both regions, although the response to shock was significantly greater in GP/SI than HDB (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the reinforcement-related response analysis presented in Figure 6E with statistical support.

claim: BFCN response latencies to reward omission were significantly slower than other reinforcement types.
source: BFCN response latencies to reward omission were significantly slower than other reinforcement types (mean ± SEM for omission vs. reward and shock; 1.04 ± 0.03 vs. 0.63 ± 0.03 s, for HDB and GP/SI, respectively; Figure 6F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the response latency analysis presented in Figure 6F with statistical support.

claim: The timing of the reward omission response was more precisely locked to lick bout offset than to timing of when reward would have been delivered.
source: The timing of the reward omission response was more precisely locked to lick bout offset than to timing of when reward would have been delivered.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal analysis of reward omission responses.

claim: Activity levels following lick bout cessation were significantly greater on reward omission trials than on trials when the reward was delivered and consumed.
source: However, the response is not likely due to movement per se, because activity levels following lick bout cessation were significantly greater on reward omission trials than on trials when the reward was delivered and consumed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lick offset analysis comparing reward and omission trials in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 with statistical support.

claim: Cue-evoked responses in HDB remained relatively constant over the remainder of conditioning, showing no significant differences between reward-related, omission-related, or punishment-related cues.
source: When compared with the Phase 1 all-rewarded stage of the operant task, cue-evoked responses in HDB remained relatively constant over the remainder of conditioning, showing no significant differences between reward-related, omission-related, or punishment-related cues (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the learning-related cue response analysis presented in Figure 7A.

claim: In GP/SI, responses to the tone frequencies associated with reward and reward omission were relatively stable.
source: In GP/SI, responses to the tone frequencies associated with reward and reward omission were also relatively stable, but cue-evoked responses for the punishment-predicting tone frequency were enhanced within a few testing sessions following the change in reinforcement outcome (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the learning-related cue response analysis presented in Figure 7B.

claim: Cue-evoked responses for the punishment-predicting tone frequency in GP/SI were enhanced within a few testing sessions following the change in reinforcement outcome.
source: In GP/SI, responses to the tone frequencies associated with reward and reward omission were also relatively stable, but cue-evoked responses for the punishment-predicting tone frequency were enhanced within a few testing sessions following the change in reinforcement outcome (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the learning-related cue response analysis presented in Figure 7B.

claim: Cue-evoked responses increased by approximately 150% in GP/SI as the animal learned a new association between sound and punishment.
source: By contrast, cue-evoked responses increased by approximately 150% in GP/SI as the animal learned a new association between sound and punishment (Figure 7C, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the learning-related cue response analysis presented in Figure 7C with quantification.

claim: When first exposed to pure tone stimuli on the initial passive characterization day, GP/SI BFCNs exhibited significantly greater within-session response habituation than HDB.
source: When first exposed to pure tone stimuli on the initial passive characterization day, GP/SI BFCNs exhibited significantly greater within-session response habituation than HDB (Figure 7E, see also Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the habituation analysis presented in Figure 7E with statistical support.

claim: Response habituation was reduced as mice became more familiar with the stimuli and task demands.
source: Response habituation was reduced as mice became more familiar with the stimuli and task demands, such that tones associated with reward or reward omission showed stable levels of reduced habituation throughout Phases 1 and 2 of the operant task (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the habituation analysis across training phases presented in Figure 7F.

claim: Strong within-session habituation was rekindled later in training, though only in GP/SI and only for the tone frequency that was remapped to punishment.
source: Interestingly, strong within-session habituation was rekindled later in training, though only in GP/SI and only for the tone frequency that was remapped to punishment (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the habituation analysis for punishment-predicting tones presented in Figure 7G.

claim: Strong, rapidly habituating responses in the caudal BFCN may reflect the neural evaluation of potentially threatening stimuli.
source: Taken as a whole, these findings suggest that strong, rapidly habituating responses in the caudal BFCN may reflect the neural evaluation of potentially threatening stimuli.
evidence: This is proposed as an interpretation of the habituation and learning-related plasticity findings.

claim: Correlating all single trial tone-evoked response amplitudes measured on each fiber reveals a very weak association (R2 = 0.16, n = 21,099 trials).
source: Correlating all single trial tone-evoked response amplitudes measured on each fiber reveals a very weak association (R2 = 0.16, n = 21,099 trials), demonstrating that the activity in HDB and GP/SI can be measured independently.
evidence: This is demonstrated by correlation analysis of simultaneous recordings from both fibers.

claim: The activity in HDB and GP/SI can be measured independently.
source: Correlating all single trial tone-evoked response amplitudes measured on each fiber reveals a very weak association (R2 = 0.16, n = 21,099 trials), demonstrating that the activity in HDB and GP/SI can be measured independently.
evidence: This is inferred from the weak correlation between simultaneous recordings from both regions.

claim: Direct visualization of efferent HDB axons showed that they left the basal forebrain in a medial and dorsal orientation, coming nowhere near the GP/SI fiber.
source: To this point, direct visualization of efferent HDB axons showed that they left the basal forebrain in a medial and dorsal orientation, coming nowhere near the GP/SI fiber (Bloem et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior anatomical study.

claim: Approximately 80% of the neurons in GP/SI are cholinergic.
source: Collectively, these findings point toward the caudal tail of the basal forebrain, which provides the strongest overall projection from the basal forebrain to ACtx and where approximately 80% of the neurons are cholinergic (Guo et al., 2019; Kamke et al., 2005; Rye et al., 1984), as a hub for encoding and associating sound with aversive, noxious stimuli, and for regulating inhibitory microcircuits within ACtx for long-term plasticity to enhance the representation of threat-predicting sounds (David et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2019; Letzkus et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The caudal tail of the basal forebrain provides the strongest overall projection from the basal forebrain to ACtx.
source: Collectively, these findings point toward the caudal tail of the basal forebrain, which provides the strongest overall projection from the basal forebrain to ACtx and where approximately 80% of the neurons are cholinergic (Guo et al., 2019; Kamke et al., 2005; Rye et al., 1984), as a hub for encoding and associating sound with aversive, noxious stimuli, and for regulating inhibitory microcircuits within ACtx for long-term plasticity to enhance the representation of threat-predicting sounds (David et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2019; Letzkus et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The caudal tail of the basal forebrain is a hub for encoding and associating sound with aversive, noxious stimuli.
source: Collectively, these findings point toward the caudal tail of the basal forebrain, which provides the strongest overall projection from the basal forebrain to ACtx and where approximately 80% of the neurons are cholinergic (Guo et al., 2019; Kamke et al., 2005; Rye et al., 1984), as a hub for encoding and associating sound with aversive, noxious stimuli, and for regulating inhibitory microcircuits within ACtx for long-term plasticity to enhance the representation of threat-predicting sounds (David et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2019; Letzkus et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The caudal tail of the basal forebrain regulates inhibitory microcircuits within ACtx for long-term plasticity to enhance the representation of threat-predicting sounds.
source: Collectively, these findings point toward the caudal tail of the basal forebrain, which provides the strongest overall projection from the basal forebrain to ACtx and where approximately 80% of the neurons are cholinergic (Guo et al., 2019; Kamke et al., 2005; Rye et al., 1984), as a hub for encoding and associating sound with aversive, noxious stimuli, and for regulating inhibitory microcircuits within ACtx for long-term plasticity to enhance the representation of threat-predicting sounds (David et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2019; Letzkus et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A neighboring region to GP/SI in the tail of the striatum receives specialized dopaminergic inputs that do not encode reward value, but rather are activated by potentially threatening sensory stimuli.
source: Interestingly, a neighboring region to GP/SI in the tail of the striatum also receive specialized dopaminergic inputs that do not encode reward value, but rather are activated by potentially threatening sensory stimuli (Menegas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Cholinergic and dopaminergic signaling in the caudal tail of the rodent basal ganglia and basal forebrain may function as a hub for encoding threatening signals and selecting adaptive threat avoidance behaviors.
source: This raises the interesting suggestion that cholinergic and dopaminergic signaling in the caudal tail of the rodent basal ganglia and basal forebrain may function as a hub for encoding threatening signals and selecting adaptive threat avoidance behaviors (Watabe-Uchida and Uchida, 2018).
evidence: This is proposed as a speculative interpretation based on the current findings and prior work.

claim: Auditory stimuli should elicit ACh release in ACtx even for sounds with no behavioral relevance.
source: Given that GP/SI is the predominant source of BFCN input to lateral neocortical regions including ACtx, one clear implication that would be important to test in future studies is that auditory stimuli – even sounds with no behavioral relevance – should elicit ACh release in ACtx.
evidence: This is proposed as a prediction based on the anatomical connectivity and functional findings.

claim: ACh acts through local ACtx microcircuits to remove the fetters that normally limit long-term associative plasticity.
source: ACh acts through local ACtx microcircuits to remove the fetters that normally limit long-term associative plasticity, thereby enabling local synaptic processes that support auditory fear memory encoding (Letzkus et al., 2015; Weinberger, 2004) and perceptual learning (Froemke et al., 2013; Takesian et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Learning-related plasticity in ACtx requires transient neuromodulatory surges and does not occur when stimuli are presented in a passive context.
source: Importantly, learning-related plasticity in ACtx requires transient neuromodulatory surges and does not occur when stimuli are presented in a passive context (Froemke, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Cholinergic regulation of cortical plasticity is not an all-or-none gating process but instead may reflect a threshold that is only exceeded when sound-evoked cholinergic inputs are themselves transiently amplified through learning.
source: This suggests that cholinergic regulation of cortical plasticity is not an all-or-none gating process but instead may reflect a threshold that is only exceeded when sound-evoked cholinergic inputs are themselves transiently amplified through learning (Figure 7C and G, Guo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing learning-related enhancement of punishment-predicting cues.

claim: Models portraying phasic cortical ACh release occurring only at times of reward, punishment, or heightened arousal need to be reevaluated, at least as they relate to the caudal tail of the basal forebrain and the ACtx.
source: Although the upstream factors that regulate BFCN plasticity and inter-regional synchrony have yet to be identified, it is clear that models portraying phasic cortical ACh release occurring only at times of reward, punishment, or heightened arousal need to be reevaluated, at least as they relate to the caudal tail of the basal forebrain and the ACtx.
evidence: This is proposed as a conclusion based on the experimental findings showing robust responses to unconditioned auditory stimuli.

claim: Learning-related enhancement of punishment-predicting cues in GP/SI may reflect the unique input this region receives from the medial geniculate and intralaminar thalamic groups.
source: As for the learning-related enhancement of punishment-predicting – but not reward-predicting cues in GP/SI – this again may reflect the unique input this region of the basal forebrain receives from the medial geniculate and intralaminar thalamic groups, which also exhibit rapid, selective, and long-lasting enhanced spiking to tones associated with aversive stimuli (Edeline and Weinberger, 1992; Weinberger, 2011).
evidence: This is proposed as an interpretation based on anatomical connectivity and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Medial geniculate and intralaminar thalamic groups exhibit rapid, selective, and long-lasting enhanced spiking to tones associated with aversive stimuli.
source: As for the learning-related enhancement of punishment-predicting – but not reward-predicting cues in GP/SI – this again may reflect the unique input this region of the basal forebrain receives from the medial geniculate and intralaminar thalamic groups, which also exhibit rapid, selective, and long-lasting enhanced spiking to tones associated with aversive stimuli (Edeline and Weinberger, 1992; Weinberger, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Learned enhancement of reward-predicting auditory cues have been observed in BFCN axons arising from more rostral basal forebrain regions that innervate the basolateral amygdala.
source: Learned enhancement of reward-predicting auditory cues have either been observed in BFCN axons arising from more rostral basal forebrain regions that innervate the basolateral amygdala (Crouse et al., 2020) and ACtx (Kuchibhotla et al., 2017), or have only been described in putative non-cholinergic neurons in HDB (Lin and Nicolelis, 2008), which therefore offers no point of contradiction with the absence of reward-related enhancement reported here in HDB and GP/SI BFCNs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Learned enhancement of reward-predicting auditory cues have been observed in BFCN axons arising from more rostral basal forebrain regions that innervate ACtx.
source: Learned enhancement of reward-predicting auditory cues have either been observed in BFCN axons arising from more rostral basal forebrain regions that innervate the basolateral amygdala (Crouse et al., 2020) and ACtx (Kuchibhotla et al., 2017), or have only been described in putative non-cholinergic neurons in HDB (Lin and Nicolelis, 2008), which therefore offers no point of contradiction with the absence of reward-related enhancement reported here in HDB and GP/SI BFCNs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Learned enhancement of reward-predicting auditory cues have only been described in putative non-cholinergic neurons in HDB.
source: Learned enhancement of reward-predicting auditory cues have either been observed in BFCN axons arising from more rostral basal forebrain regions that innervate the basolateral amygdala (Crouse et al., 2020) and ACtx (Kuchibhotla et al., 2017), or have only been described in putative non-cholinergic neurons in HDB (Lin and Nicolelis, 2008), which therefore offers no point of contradiction with the absence of reward-related enhancement reported here in HDB and GP/SI BFCNs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: HDB and GP/SI BFCNs may have exhibited an increased response to reward-predicting cues during the initial association of sound and reward, which occurred during the behavioral shaping period when activity was not monitored.
source: As mentioned above, another possibility is that HDB and GP/SI BFCNs did exhibit an increased response to reward-predicting cues during the initial association of sound and reward, which occurred during the behavioral shaping period when we did not monitor activity.
evidence: This is proposed as an alternative explanation for the absence of observed learning-related enhancement for reward-predicting cues.

claim: Rostral and caudal BFCN responses share many similarities in their response features, particularly as they relate to arousal and reinforcement.
source: Collectively, our findings support the view that rostral and caudal BFCN responses share many similarities in their response features, particularly as they relate to arousal and reinforcement, yet regional afferent and efferent connectivity differences – particularly in the caudal tail of the basal forebrain – support regional specializations for encoding sensory salience and expressing associative plasticity during aversive reinforcement learning.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Regional afferent and efferent connectivity differences in the caudal tail of the basal forebrain support regional specializations for encoding sensory salience and expressing associative plasticity during aversive reinforcement learning.
source: Collectively, our findings support the view that rostral and caudal BFCN responses share many similarities in their response features, particularly as they relate to arousal and reinforcement, yet regional afferent and efferent connectivity differences – particularly in the caudal tail of the basal forebrain – support regional specializations for encoding sensory salience and expressing associative plasticity during aversive reinforcement learning.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings and anatomical knowledge.

claim: Fiber-based imaging was the best methodology to address the experimental aims of performing simultaneous measurements of rostral and caudal BFCNs over an extended period.
source: From a technical perspective, fiber-based imaging was the best methodology to address our experimental aims, particularly for the goal of performing simultaneous measurements of rostral and caudal BFCNs over an extended period.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological justification.

claim: BFCNs in GP/SI are arrayed in a thin dorsoventral sheet along the lateral wall of the internal capsule and then split into thin vertically oriented arrangements along the medial and lateral boundaries of the external GP.
source: BFCNs in GP/SI are arrayed in a thin dorsoventral sheet along the lateral wall of the internal capsule and then split into thin vertically oriented arrangements along the medial and lateral boundaries of the external GP (Clayton et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: The anatomy of BFCNs in GP/SI is not optimal for endoscopic imaging through implanted lenses, as it could be challenging to visualize BFCNs in a single focal plane.
source: This anatomy is not optimal for endoscopic imaging through implanted lenses, as it could be challenging to visualize BFCNs in a single focal plane.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical description and technical considerations.

claim: Two-photon imaging of the cortical axon terminals from GP/SI BFCNs is feasible.
source: Two-photon imaging of the cortical axon terminals from GP/SI BFCNs is feasible (Nelson and Mooney, 2016), though these signals would still arise from an indeterminate number of neurons and concerns about tissue bleaching and photodamage would not be compatible with the hours of daily testing over 30+ consecutive days that was performed here.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study but with noted limitations.

claim: Antidromic or somatic optogenetic tagging of single BFCNs is the gold standard, affording the highest level of spatial and temporal resolution.
source: Antidromic or somatic optogenetic tagging of single BFCNs is the gold standard, affording the highest level of spatial and temporal resolution.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The yield of antidromic optogenetic tagging for GP/SI BFCNs that project to ACtx was punishingly low (~1% of all units recorded).
source: Our prior work used the antidromic variant of this approach to make targeted single unit recordings from GP/SI BFCNs that project to ACtx, but the yield was punishingly low (~1% of all units recorded) and units could not be held long enough to measure responses to all of the experimental variables tested here (Guo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is reported from prior work by the authors.

claim: The slow temporal kinetics and poor spatial resolution of fiber-based GCaMP imaging combines somatic and neuropil-based calcium signals and obscures the relationship to spike rates in distinct types of BFCNs.
source: Another caveat in the interpretation of fiber-based GCaMP imaging is that the slow temporal kinetics and poor spatial resolution combines somatic and neuropil-based calcium signals and obscures the relationship to spike rates in distinct types of BFCNs.
evidence: This is stated as a known technical limitation of the method.

claim: Anatomical characterizations suggest that BFCN inputs within the basal forebrain primarily arise from local neurons rather than remote regions.
source: Further, anatomical characterizations suggest that BFCN inputs within the basal forebrain primarily arise from local neurons rather than remote regions (Gielow and Zaborszky, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior anatomical study.

claim: BFCNs within nucleus basalis and HDB can be subdivided into bursting and regular-firing BFCNs.
source: An elegant recent study has demonstrated that BFCNs within nucleus basalis and HDB are not an indivisible class, but can themselves be further subdivided into bursting and regular-firing BFCNs, where the proportion of each type varied across the rostral-caudal extent of the basal forebrain and had distinct patterns of synchronization both with respect to each other and with network oscillations measured in ACtx (Laszlovszky et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: The spike timing of bursting BFCNs showed a stronger coupling with the ACtx on trials where mice made a Go response.
source: Interestingly, when studied in the context of an auditory task similar to the paradigm used here, the spike timing of bursting BFCNs showed a stronger coupling with the ACtx on trials where mice made a Go response (regardless of whether it was a hit or false positive) whereas the regular-firing BFCNs showed a stronger coupling with the ACtx on trials where mice made the correct response (regardless of whether it was Go or NoGo).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: The spike timing of regular-firing BFCNs showed a stronger coupling with the ACtx on trials where mice made the correct response.
source: Interestingly, when studied in the context of an auditory task similar to the paradigm used here, the spike timing of bursting BFCNs showed a stronger coupling with the ACtx on trials where mice made a Go response (regardless of whether it was a hit or false positive) whereas the regular-firing BFCNs showed a stronger coupling with the ACtx on trials where mice made the correct response (regardless of whether it was Go or NoGo).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Prior studies have reported that cholinergic levels prior to auditory onset can predict whether the animal would subsequently produce the correct or incorrect operant response.
source: Prior studies have also reported that cholinergic levels prior to auditory onset can predict whether the animal would subsequently produce the correct or incorrect operant response, suggesting the bulk measures may be sensitive to pre-cue dynamics that are not resolvable at the level of single neurons (Kuchibhotla et al., 2017; Parikh et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Hit or miss trial outcomes in a challenging auditory detection task could be predicted from the degree of synchrony in local networks of ACtx layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons measured from a 1 s period prior to the delivery of the auditory cue.
source: In a recent study, we found that hit or miss trial outcomes in a challenging auditory detection task could be predicted from the degree of synchrony in local networks of ACtx layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons measured from a 1 s period prior to the delivery of the auditory cue (Resnik and Polley, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: The cholinergic basal forebrain has classically been studied as a master regulator of cortical network synchrony.
source: As the cholinergic basal forebrain has classically been studied as a master regulator of cortical network synchrony (Buzsaki et al., 1988; Metherate et al., 1992), one clear suggestion is that ongoing cholinergic dynamics in the period preceding environmental sensory cues strongly regulate cortical network state, which can have profound impacts on the accurate encoding of sensory cues and appropriate selection of cue-directed actions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Ongoing cholinergic dynamics in the period preceding environmental sensory cues strongly regulate cortical network state.
source: As the cholinergic basal forebrain has classically been studied as a master regulator of cortical network synchrony (Buzsaki et al., 1988; Metherate et al., 1992), one clear suggestion is that ongoing cholinergic dynamics in the period preceding environmental sensory cues strongly regulate cortical network state, which can have profound impacts on the accurate encoding of sensory cues and appropriate selection of cue-directed actions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and prior knowledge.

claim: Cortical network state can have profound impacts on the accurate encoding of sensory cues and appropriate selection of cue-directed actions.
source: As the cholinergic basal forebrain has classically been studied as a master regulator of cortical network synchrony (Buzsaki et al., 1988; Metherate et al., 1992), one clear suggestion is that ongoing cholinergic dynamics in the period preceding environmental sensory cues strongly regulate cortical network state, which can have profound impacts on the accurate encoding of sensory cues and appropriate selection of cue-directed actions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing pre-cue activity predicts behavioral outcomes.
